cluster.name: Delhi-Agra
cluster.summary: The densest concentration of World Heritage architecture in India: Mughal Agra and eight centuries of layered Delhi, roughly 230 km apart and linked by expressway and fast trains. Winter is the season; May-June heat is genuinely dangerous for outdoor sightseeing.
cluster.intercity_hub: Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) / New Delhi Railway Station

attractions.name: Taj Mahal
attractions.summary: Shah Jahan's white-marble mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal, completed in 1653 and the defining monument of Mughal architecture.
attractions.history: Shah Jahan commissioned the tomb in 1632 after the death of his wife Mumtaz Mahal in childbirth, and the mausoleum was substantially complete by 1643 with the wider complex finished around 1653. Ustad Ahmad Lahauri is generally credited as the chief architect. Marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan and the inlaid stones from as far as Afghanistan, Tibet and Sri Lanka.
attractions.significance: The Taj is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the culmination of Indo-Islamic funerary architecture: a perfectly symmetrical charbagh garden tomb where the mausoleum is placed at the end rather than the centre, so that it is silhouetted against sky rather than enclosed by garden. Its pietra dura inlay and calligraphy - which subtly increases in size with height so the letters appear uniform from below - remain technically unmatched.
interesting_facts: The Quranic calligraphy on the entrance arch grows progressively larger with height so it reads as uniform from ground level.
The four minarets tilt very slightly outwards so that they would fall away from the tomb in an earthquake.
The marble changes apparent colour through the day - pink at dawn, white at midday, amber at sunset.
The complex closes to general visitors on Fridays for congregational prayers at the mosque.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Wheelchairs are available free at the entrance and the garden paths are level. The main plinth is reached by a long ramp, but the inner chamber has a raised threshold. Battery buses cover the distance from the parking area to the gates.
attractions.dress_code: No formal dress code, but shoe covers (provided with the ticket) must be worn on the marble plinth.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography is permitted in the gardens but strictly prohibited inside the main mausoleum chamber. Tripods and drones are not allowed.
local_customs: Only small bags are allowed; food, tobacco and large electronics must be left in lockers.
Shoe covers are mandatory on the plinth.
Do not touch the inlay work.

schedule.note: Sunrise to sunset; night viewing runs separately around full moon

costs.note: Base ticket plus optional mausoleum surcharge

attractions.verification_note: Closed Fridays. Ticket tiers, night-viewing dates and entry gates change - verify with the official ASI portal before visiting.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Taj Mahal

attractions.name: Agra Fort
attractions.summary: A red sandstone walled city of the Mughals, rebuilt by Akbar from 1565 and later remodelled in marble by Shah Jahan.
attractions.history: Akbar began rebuilding the earlier Lodi-era fort in red sandstone in 1565, creating a walled imperial city on the Yamuna. Jahangir and Shah Jahan added marble pavilions, and Shah Jahan was eventually imprisoned here by his son Aurangzeb, reputedly with a view of the Taj Mahal from the Musamman Burj.
attractions.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site, Agra Fort is the clearest built record of the Mughal shift from Akbar's robust sandstone idiom to Shah Jahan's refined marble aesthetic - the two styles stand side by side within one enclosure. Roughly a quarter of the fort is open to visitors; the rest remains with the Indian Army.
interesting_facts: The double walls rise about 21 metres and run for around 2.5 km.
Shah Jahan spent his final years imprisoned in the Musamman Burj, which looks toward the Taj.
The Sheesh Mahal is lined with thousands of tiny mirror tiles designed to multiply candlelight.
Part of the fort is still an active military installation and closed to the public.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The long ramped entrance causeway is navigable with assistance and much of the main courtyard level is flat, but several pavilions require steps. Wheelchairs are available at the gate.
attractions.dress_code: No restriction; sun protection strongly advised.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted. Video cameras may incur a charge; drones prohibited.
local_customs: Do not photograph the army-controlled sections or personnel.
The ramped approach is steep - pace yourself in the heat.
attractions.verification_note: ASI ticket rates are revised by notification - verify before visiting.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Agra Fort

attractions.name: Fatehpur Sikri
attractions.summary: Akbar's purpose-built capital of 1571, abandoned within about fifteen years and preserved almost intact in red sandstone.
attractions.history: Akbar founded the city in 1571 near the hermitage of the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, whose blessing was credited with the birth of Akbar's heir. It served as the Mughal capital for roughly fourteen years before being abandoned, most likely because of an inadequate water supply. Because it was never reoccupied or substantially rebuilt, its buildings survive as a coherent late-sixteenth-century ensemble.
attractions.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site, Fatehpur Sikri is the fullest surviving expression of Akbar's syncretic imperial vision: Hindu, Jain, Islamic and Persian structural and decorative forms combined in one planned city. The Buland Darwaza, at roughly 54 metres, is among the tallest gateways in the world, and the Diwan-i-Khas contains a unique single central pillar supporting a radial platform.
interesting_facts: The Buland Darwaza was built to commemorate Akbar's Gujarat campaign.
The Diwan-i-Khas has one carved central column supporting four radiating bridges - a design found nowhere else.
A giant pachisi (board game) court is laid into the courtyard paving, said to have been played with people as pieces.
The city was abandoned after only about fifteen years, most likely due to water shortage.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The main palace complex is largely level once inside, but the approach from the parking area is on a slope and the Jama Masjid courtyard is reached by a long flight of steps at the Buland Darwaza.
attractions.dress_code: Head covering required in the Jama Masjid and at the Salim Chishti dargah; footwear must be removed there.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted throughout; drones prohibited.
local_customs: Footwear must be removed on the mosque courtyard - the sandstone gets extremely hot; carry socks.
Unofficial guides are persistent; use only ASI-approved guides.
Tying a thread at the Salim Chishti tomb is a local tradition, not an obligation.

schedule.note: The Jama Masjid and dargah keep separate timings and remain open on Fridays

attractions.verification_note: The mosque complex and the ASI palace complex have different ticketing and hours - verify before visiting.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Fatehpur Sikri

attractions.name: Itmad-ud-Daulah's Tomb (Baby Taj)
attractions.summary: The first Mughal building faced entirely in white marble, and the earliest large-scale use of pietra dura inlay in India.
attractions.history: Nur Jahan built the tomb between 1622 and 1628 for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg, a Persian noble who rose to be Jahangir's treasurer with the title Itmad-ud-Daulah. Its marble facing and inlaid semiprecious stone directly anticipate the Taj Mahal, built a generation later.
attractions.significance: This is the pivotal building in Mughal architecture: the point at which red sandstone gave way to white marble and at which pietra dura inlay replaced carved relief as the primary decorative technique. Without it the Taj Mahal's vocabulary would not exist.
interesting_facts: It is often called the 'Baby Taj' or the 'draft' of the Taj Mahal.
Nur Jahan, who commissioned it, was the most politically powerful woman of the Mughal court.
The jali screens are carved from single marble slabs.
It sits on the quieter east bank of the Yamuna and is far less crowded than the Taj.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Garden paths are level; the tomb platform is reached by a short flight of steps.
attractions.dress_code: No restriction; footwear removed on the marble platform.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted including inside the chamber.
local_customs: Remove footwear before stepping onto the marble plinth.
attractions.verification_note: ASI rates revised by notification - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Mehtab Bagh
attractions.summary: A Mughal riverfront garden directly across the Yamuna from the Taj Mahal, and the classic sunset viewpoint.
attractions.history: The garden was laid out in the early Mughal period, likely under Babur, and was later aligned precisely with the Taj Mahal complex across the river. Long buried under silt, it was excavated and replanted by the ASI in the 1990s, which confirmed that it was designed as the visual counterpart to the mausoleum.
attractions.significance: Mehtab Bagh completes the Taj's intended composition: the mausoleum was meant to be seen reflected in a pool from this garden. It is also the last of eleven Mughal gardens that once lined this stretch of the Yamuna.
interesting_facts: The garden's central axis lines up exactly with the Taj Mahal's dome.
An octagonal pool here was designed to hold the Taj's reflection.
The persistent story of a 'Black Taj' planned on this bank is not supported by archaeological evidence.
It offers the only unobstructed sunset view of the Taj from ground level.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Compacted gravel paths are mostly level but can be soft after rain.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; tripods generally allowed here, unlike inside the Taj complex.
local_customs: The garden closes at sunset - arrive at least 45 minutes before.
attractions.verification_note: Closing time tracks sunset and shifts through the year - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Humayun's Tomb
attractions.summary: The first great Mughal garden tomb in India, built in 1570 and the direct architectural ancestor of the Taj Mahal.
attractions.history: Commissioned by Humayun's widow Bega Begum and completed around 1570, the tomb was designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas. It introduced the charbagh garden tomb to India and established the red-sandstone-with-white-marble palette that defined Mughal building for a century. A major conservation programme in the 2000s restored the gardens and water channels.
attractions.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site and the prototype for every subsequent Mughal mausoleum, including the Taj Mahal. It is also a dense necropolis: more than a hundred Mughal family members are buried in the complex, and the surrounding precinct includes Isa Khan's tomb, which predates Humayun's by twenty years.
interesting_facts: It was the first structure in India to use a double dome - an outer shell for silhouette and an inner one scaled to the chamber.
Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, was captured here by the British in 1857.
Isa Khan's octagonal tomb inside the complex predates the main mausoleum by about two decades.
The restoration reinstated the original garden water channels using traditional techniques.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Garden paths are wide and level and a ramp reaches the plinth on one side; the inner chamber has raised thresholds. Wheelchairs are available at the ticket office.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; tripods and drones need permission.
local_customs: Remove footwear before entering the marble cenotaph chamber.
attractions.verification_note: ASI rates revised by notification - verify before visiting.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Humayun's Tomb

attractions.name: Qutb Minar Complex
attractions.summary: A 72.5 m fluted victory tower begun in 1193, standing over the earliest Islamic architecture in northern India.
attractions.history: Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the minaret in 1193 to mark the establishment of Delhi Sultanate rule, and it was completed in stages by his successors, notably Iltutmish and Firoz Shah Tughlaq. The adjoining Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, the first congregational mosque built in northern India, reused columns from earlier temples on the site.
attractions.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site and the founding monument of Indo-Islamic architecture in India. The complex documents the transition from Hindu structural techniques and craft vocabulary to Islamic architectural forms - the earliest arches here are corbelled rather than true arches, because local masons had not yet learned voussoir construction.
interesting_facts: At 72.5 metres it is the tallest brick minaret in the world.
The 7 m Iron Pillar in the courtyard, dating to roughly the fourth century CE, has resisted rust for over 1,600 years due to its phosphorus content.
The tower narrows from about 14.3 m at the base to 2.7 m at the top.
Interior access to the minaret has been closed to the public since a stampede in 1981.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Main lawns and paved routes are level and largely wheelchair-navigable; the mosque courtyard has uneven historic paving and steps.
local_customs: The minaret interior is permanently closed - do not attempt to enter.
Do not climb on the ruins.
attractions.verification_note: ASI rates revised by notification - verify before visiting.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Qutb Minar

attractions.name: Red Fort (Lal Qila)
attractions.summary: Shah Jahan's imperial citadel of 1648, from whose ramparts the Prime Minister addresses the nation each Independence Day.
attractions.history: Built between 1638 and 1648 as the palace fort of Shahjahanabad, Shah Jahan's new capital, the Red Fort was the Mughal seat of power until 1857. After the revolt of 1857 the British demolished a large part of its interior palaces and converted the site into a garrison, which is why the surviving buildings sit in unusually open ground.
attractions.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site and the symbolic centre of modern Indian statehood: the national flag has been raised here every Independence Day since 1947. Architecturally, the Diwan-i-Khas and the marble pavilions of the riverside range represent the peak of Shah Jahani decorative work.
interesting_facts: The Persian couplet in the Diwan-i-Khas reads: 'If there be a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this.'
The Peacock Throne stood here until Nadir Shah carried it to Persia in 1739.
A water channel called the Nahr-i-Behisht - Stream of Paradise - ran through the palace pavilions.
The fort is closed to visitors on Mondays.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Long level walkways connect the main pavilions and are wheelchair-navigable, but the distances are considerable and the covered bazaar has a slight gradient.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted. Security screening is strict; drones and large bags are prohibited.
local_customs: Security checks are thorough - allow extra time.
Closed on Mondays and around Independence Day preparations.
attractions.verification_note: Closed Mondays; access is restricted around national days - verify before visiting.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre - Red Fort Complex

attractions.name: Jama Masjid
attractions.summary: India's largest congregational mosque, completed in 1656, with a courtyard for twenty-five thousand worshippers.
attractions.history: Shah Jahan commissioned the mosque, originally named Masjid-i Jahan-Numa, between 1650 and 1656 as the principal mosque of Shahjahanabad. Built of red sandstone and white marble on a raised plinth, it was designed to be approached by broad flights of steps from three sides so that it dominated the surrounding city.
attractions.significance: The mosque remains the central congregational space of Old Delhi and one of the defining works of Shah Jahani architecture. Climbing the southern minaret gives the best available panorama over the Old Delhi rooftops and the Red Fort.
interesting_facts: The courtyard can hold about twenty-five thousand worshippers.
The northern gate houses relics traditionally attributed to the Prophet Muhammad.
The southern minaret can be climbed by a narrow spiral staircase for a rooftop view of Old Delhi.
The three marble domes are striped with black marble inlay.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The mosque sits on a high plinth reached by long flights of steps on all approaches, with no ramp or lift. The minaret climb is a narrow spiral staircase.
attractions.dress_code: Strictly modest dress. Shoulders, arms and legs must be covered; women must cover their heads. Robes are available to borrow at the gate for a charge. Footwear must be removed.
attractions.photography_policy: A camera charge applies. Photography during prayers is not permitted.
local_customs: Closed to sightseers during the five daily prayers and Friday midday prayer.
The stone courtyard becomes extremely hot barefoot in summer - visit early or late.
Do not walk in front of people praying.

schedule.note: Closed to visitors around each prayer time; longer closure Friday midday

attractions.verification_note: Visiting windows depend on daily prayer times, which shift through the year - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: India Gate & Kartavya Path
attractions.summary: Lutyens' 42 m war memorial arch at the end of the ceremonial axis of New Delhi, with the National War Memorial behind it.
attractions.history: Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and completed in 1931, the arch commemorates around 70,000 Indian soldiers who died in the First World War and the Third Anglo-Afghan War; more than 13,000 names are inscribed on its surfaces. The Amar Jawan Jyoti flame was added after the 1971 war, and in 2022 was merged with the flame at the adjacent National War Memorial.
attractions.significance: India Gate anchors the ceremonial axis of Lutyens' New Delhi, running from Rashtrapati Bhavan through Vijay Chowk. The renamed Kartavya Path is the route of the annual Republic Day parade and functions as the country's principal ceremonial public space.
interesting_facts: More than 13,000 servicemen's names are carved on the arch.
The canopy behind the arch once held a statue of George V, removed after independence.
The lawns are a popular evening picnic spot for Delhi families.
The National War Memorial, opened in 2019, sits just behind and commemorates post-independence conflicts.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The redeveloped Kartavya Path has wide level paved walkways, accessible toilets and ramped crossings throughout.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted. Do not photograph security installations. Drones are prohibited across central Delhi.
local_customs: The National War Memorial is a place of remembrance - maintain decorum and do not picnic there.
Vehicle access is restricted; expect a walk from parking.

schedule.note: Open space; the National War Memorial keeps separate hours

attractions.verification_note: Free public space; access is restricted in the weeks around Republic Day.

attractions.name: Lotus Temple (Bahai House of Worship)
attractions.summary: A Bahai house of worship of 1986 shaped as a nine-sided lotus in twenty-seven marble petals, open to all faiths.
attractions.history: Designed by the Iranian-Canadian architect Fariborz Sahba and completed in 1986, the temple uses twenty-seven free-standing marble-clad petals arranged in clusters of three to form nine sides. Bahai houses of worship are always nine-sided and have no idols, altars, pulpits or clergy.
attractions.significance: The building is among the most-visited structures in the world and has received multiple international architectural awards for its structural engineering. As a place of worship it is deliberately non-denominational: scripture from any faith may be read aloud, but no sermons, rituals or musical instruments are permitted.
interesting_facts: Twenty-seven marble petals form the nine sides required of every Bahai temple.
The marble is Pentelic marble from Greece, the same source used for the Parthenon.
The building uses natural ventilation and daylight, with pools that cool incoming air.
Anyone of any faith may enter and pray; only silence is required.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A dedicated accessible route and lift avoid the main steps; wheelchairs are available and volunteers assist. Queues can be bypassed for visitors with mobility needs - ask a volunteer.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear must be removed and deposited before entering the prayer hall.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography is permitted in the gardens but strictly prohibited inside the prayer hall.
local_customs: Complete silence is required inside the hall.
No sermons, rituals, offerings or music are permitted.
Queues are often long; arriving at opening time is the best strategy.

costs.note: Free entry; no donations accepted from non-Bahais

attractions.verification_note: Closed Mondays; summer and winter timings differ - verify before visiting.

sources.title: Bahai House of Worship, New Delhi - official

attractions.name: National Museum
attractions.summary: India's principal national collection, from Harappan seals and the Dancing Girl to Chola bronzes and Mughal miniatures.
attractions.history: The museum grew out of an exhibition of Indian art shown in London in 1947-48, which on its return was displayed in Rashtrapati Bhavan and then given a permanent building on Janpath, inaugurated in 1960. It holds roughly two hundred thousand objects spanning five thousand years.
attractions.significance: This is the reference collection for Indian material culture: the Harappan gallery holds the bronze Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro, and the Buddhist gallery holds relics attributed to the Buddha recovered from Piprahwa. For anyone visiting Delhi's monuments, a morning here supplies the chronology that makes the sites legible.
interesting_facts: The bronze Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro, about 4,500 years old, is the museum's signature object.
The Buddhist gallery holds relics excavated at Piprahwa and attributed to the Buddha.
The Chola bronze collection includes major Nataraja figures.
It is fully air-conditioned, which makes it the best option during a Delhi heatwave.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Ramped entrance and lifts to all galleries; wheelchairs available at reception. Fully air-conditioned.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography without flash is generally permitted in most galleries; some loaned exhibits are restricted.
local_customs: Bags must be deposited in the cloakroom.
Audio guides are available and worth taking.

schedule.note: Closed on Mondays and national holidays

costs.note: Free for students with valid ID

attractions.verification_note: Closed Mondays; gallery closures for renovation are common - verify before visiting.

sources.title: National Museum, New Delhi - Ministry of Culture

attractions.name: Chandni Chowk & Khari Baoli
attractions.summary: Shahjahanabad's main street of 1650, still a working bazaar, with Asia's largest wholesale spice market at its western end.
attractions.history: Laid out around 1650 under the supervision of Jahanara Begum, Shah Jahan's eldest daughter, the street originally had a canal running down its centre that reflected moonlight - the origin of the name 'moonlit square'. Khari Baoli, at its western end, has traded spices since the seventeenth century.
attractions.significance: Chandni Chowk is the oldest continuously trading market street in Delhi and the commercial heart of Mughal Shahjahanabad. Within a few hundred metres it contains a Jain temple with a bird hospital, a Sikh gurdwara marking a martyrdom site, a Hindu temple, a church and a mosque - a concentration of religious plurality unusual anywhere.
interesting_facts: The name means 'moonlit square', from the canal that once reflected moonlight along its length.
The Jain temple at the eastern end runs a charitable bird hospital.
Khari Baoli is described as the largest wholesale spice market in Asia.
Paranthe Wali Gali, a lane of fried-bread shops, has operated since the nineteenth century.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Extremely congested lanes, uneven surfaces, open drains in places and constant cycle-rickshaw traffic. Not practical for wheelchair users or anyone with significant mobility limits.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress; head covering needed to enter the gurdwara.
attractions.photography_policy: Ask before photographing traders. Photography inside religious buildings follows each institution's rules.
local_customs: Cover your head and remove footwear at Gurdwara Sis Ganj.
Bargaining is normal in the retail lanes but not at food stalls.
Guard valuables closely - the crowd density is extreme.
Most wholesale shops close on Sundays.

schedule.note: Khari Baoli opens earlier; most shops closed on Sundays

attractions.verification_note: Shop timings and Sunday closures vary by trade - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Raj Ghat
attractions.summary: The cremation memorial of Mahatma Gandhi: a black marble platform with an eternal flame, set in quiet lawns.
attractions.history: Raj Ghat marks the place where Mahatma Gandhi was cremated on 31 January 1948, the day after his assassination. The memorial is a simple square platform of black marble, deliberately unadorned, inscribed with his last words. Adjacent memorials commemorate Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi and other national leaders.
attractions.significance: Raj Ghat is the primary site of official state remembrance in India; visiting heads of state lay wreaths here. Its deliberate architectural restraint - no dome, no statue, no ornament - was a design choice consistent with Gandhi's own principles.
interesting_facts: The platform is inscribed with the words 'Hey Ram', reported as Gandhi's last utterance.
An eternal flame burns at one end of the platform.
Visiting foreign dignitaries traditionally plant a tree in the surrounding grounds.
Footwear must be removed before approaching the memorial platform.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Level paved paths lead to the memorial enclosure; the final platform approach is step-free.
attractions.dress_code: No formal dress code, but this is a memorial - dress and behave respectfully. Footwear removed at the enclosure.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; be discreet during ceremonies.
local_customs: Remove footwear before entering the memorial enclosure.
Maintain silence near the platform.
Prayer meetings are held on Fridays.
attractions.verification_note: Free entry; access may be restricted during state ceremonies.
